title: Bacterial–algal biofilm treatment of 2,4‐dimethylphenol: Comparative performance of four reactor configurations
content:
Abstract

The treatment of highly toxic and refractory phenolic wastewater remains challenging because conventional biological processes can be strongly inhibited at high pollutant concentrations. In this study, four reactor configurations were compared: a non-aerated suspended-sludge control reactor (R1), a non-aerated polyurethane (PU)-supported biofilm reactor (R2), a PU-supported Chlorella biofilm reactor (R3), and a PU-supported bacterial–algal biofilm reactor (R4). With initial concentrations of 230 mg/L 2,4-dimethylphenol (2,4-DMP) and 60 mg/L NH4 +-N, R4 achieved 92.20% 2,4-DMP removal and 98.50% chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal at 64 h, showing the highest observed removal efficiencies among the four reactor configurations. The NH4 +-N removal efficiency of R4 reached 43.98% at 64 h. R1 maintained relatively high bulk dissolved oxygen (DO) while showing poor pollutant removal, whereas the Chlorella-containing reactors exhibited substantially higher treatment efficiencies under relatively low bulk DO conditions, indicating that bulk DO alone did not determine reactor performance. Scanning electron microscopy provided morphological evidence for the coexistence of bacterial- and algal-like structures on the PU carrier in R4. The Chlorella-containing biofilm configuration may provide a basis for future biomass-oriented resource recovery; however, biomass yield, growth, biochemical composition, and energy content were not quantified in the present study. Overall, the results demonstrate the laboratory-scale potential of a PU-supported bacterial–algal biofilm for treating high-strength 2,4-DMP wastewater, while further validation under shorter reaction cycles and real-wastewater conditions is needed for engineering application.
